turns.text:
## What the data actually shows

Using compute_metric (net_contribution and channel_spend, metric definitions from list_metrics) for the quarter just ended (Q2 2026, 2026‑04‑01 to 2026‑07‑01), and counting leads directly (lead.via_channel edges):

- **Channel B**: $800 spend → 40 leads (LD00460–LD00499) → $10,000 net contribution → **$250/lead**, $20 cost/lead.
- **Channel A**: $1,000 spend → 100 leads (LD00360–LD00459) → $7,000 net contribution → **$70/lead**, $10 cost/lead.

So the $250 vs $70 numbers check out exactly against last quarter's ledger. On a per-dollar-spent basis B does look far better (12.5x return vs 7x).

## Why I would not just double it

1. **No historical evidence at higher spend.** I checked channel_spend for every quarter back to 2025‑01‑01: it has been flat at exactly $800/quarter for B and $1,000/quarter for A for six straight quarters. There is no quarter in the data where B's spend was ever different, so we have zero observed evidence of what cost-per-lead or net-contribution-per-lead does when spend rises. The $250/lead figure is an average at the current spend level, not a proven marginal return — channels commonly get more expensive per lead (or hit worse-fit prospects) as spend scales up.

2. **A real capacity constraint shows up in this quarter's data.** Technician utilisation (tech_utilisation_pct, Q2 2026) shows one technician, Rafa Osei, at 94% of his 520 available quarterly hours, while four other techs sit at 3.85%. Rafa is one of only two people certified for the "backflow" service line (person.holds → certification:backflow-tester), and the other certified tech, Tomas Bell, has had no jobs assigned since 2026‑02‑18 — effectively inactive this quarter. I traced one of this quarter's channel‑B leads (LD00460) straight through to a backflow job (J00114), so at least part of channel B's demand lands on exactly the service line that's already nearly maxed out on certified labor. Under the shop's own scheduling policy, a technician can only be put on a job in a line he's certified for — so extra channel‑B leads that need backflow work can't just be handed to an idle tech; they'd wait or go unfulfilled, which means they wouldn't actually deliver $250 each.

## What the extra $800 would bring in, stated plainly

- **If B scales linearly** (same $20 cost/lead, same $250 net contribution/lead as this quarter): +$800 → roughly 40 more leads → roughly **$10,000** more net contribution. That is the optimistic, unverified number — it assumes the channel doesn't get more expensive and that every extra lead can actually be staffed.
- **What's missing to trust that number**: (a) any quarter where B's spend actually varied, to see real marginal cost/lead and marginal conversion, and (b) confirmation of what share of B's job mix is backflow vs. other service lines, plus a plan for the certified-labor bottleneck (reactivate Tomas Bell, certify another tech, or confirm B's leads mostly land in lines with spare capacity like the 3.85%-utilised techs).

## Recommendation

Don't double blindly. Run a smaller step-up first (e.g. +25–50%) to observe real marginal cost/lead and conversion, and in parallel pull the service-line mix for channel B's jobs and resolve the backflow capacity gap. This is an internal analysis, not a customer-facing message, so no owner approval is needed to think it through — approval would only be needed before scheduling anything that runs into the "certified tech only" and "over‑8‑hour job" policies, or before sending anything to a customer.

ANSWER: Last quarter B genuinely earned $250/lead vs A's $70/lead, but spend has never varied (flat $800/$1,000 per quarter for six quarters), so that per-lead figure is an average, not a proven marginal return, and one of B's own job types (backflow) already has its only active certified technician at 94% utilisation this quarter, meaning extra B leads may not be fulfillable at that same value. Naive doubling of B's spend (+$800) would nominally forecast about 40 more leads and about $10,000 more net contribution if the channel scales exactly like this quarter, but I'd test a smaller increase first and fix the certified-capacity constraint before committing the full $800.
